q: A site moves from one server to two behind a load balancer. Sam logs in, and his next click shows "please log in". Why?
options: The load balancer deletes cookies
Sam's password expired between the two clicks
The login note was kept in the memory of one server, and the next click landed on the other one
Two servers cannot share a database
why: A server that keeps the session in its own memory is not stateless. The cookie finds nothing on the other server. Move the note to a shared box, such as the database or Redis, so any server can answer.

q: To stop the random logouts, a team turns on sticky sessions, so each user always reaches the same server. Server A restarts for an update. What happens?
options: Every user glued to Server A is logged out
Nothing, the load balancer remembers every session
Only users who were idle are logged out
Server B takes over the sessions by itself
why: Glue is not a fix, because the login still lives in one server's memory. When that server stops, those users lose it. New machines also only get new users, so adding machines helps less.

q: Your site peaks at 300 requests a second, and one simple server answers about 1,000. A teammate says "horizontal scaling is more modern, let's add ten servers." What is the best answer?
options: Agree, more servers are always safer
Scale up, because a bigger machine is always cheaper
Add a cache first, because the traffic is too high
Neither yet. One machine is enough, so scale when the numbers or a need for a spare ask for it
why: Scaling out adds a load balancer, a shared box and new ways to fail. Use the numbers. Scale up first, and scale out when you need a spare machine or you are near the limit.

q: You run 5 machines and want the site to survive losing one. At most how busy can each machine be?
options: 100 percent, because the load balancer fixes it
80 percent, because the 4 left must carry the work of 5
50 percent, because half should always be spare
60 percent, because 3 of 5 must stay free
why: The safe level is (N minus 1) divided by N, so (5 minus 1) / 5 is 80 percent. The more machines you have, the less you waste on spares.

q: A chat app does 200 requests a second, which one machine could handle, but it must keep working when one machine dies. Up or out?
options: Scale up, because 200 is a small load
Scale up, because a bigger machine never fails
Scale out to at least two machines, because the need is a spare, not the load
Neither, because chat apps cannot be scaled
why: The rule here is not the load, it is the spare. One machine is one part that stops everything. First make the servers stateless, with sessions in a shared box, then add the second machine.

q: A team moves all sessions into Redis and says "Redis holds the sessions, so we are done." What is still missing?
options: Nothing, Redis never stops
Redis is now the one part that stops everything, so it needs a spare copy that takes over
The sessions should go back into server memory
A second load balancer in front of Redis
why: You moved the single point of failure, you did not remove it. Every request now also takes a small trip to the shared box, and if the box fails, every user is logged out.
